claim: Tumor cells excrete large quantities of fermentation products in the presence of sufficient oxygen.
source: A prominent feature of cancer metabolism is that tumor cells excrete large quantities of fermentation products in the presence of sufficient oxygen (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on cancer metabolism

claim: The Warburg effect was discovered by Otto Warburg in the 1920s.
source: This process, discovered by Otto Warburg in the 1920s (Warburg, 1924) and known as the Warburg effect, aerobic glycolysis, or overflow metabolism (Basan et al., 2015; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009), is ubiquitous among fast-proliferating cells across a broad spectrum of organisms (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), ranging from bacteria (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Meyer et al., 1984; Nanchen et al., 2006; Neidhardt et al., 1990) and fungi (De Deken, 1966) to mammalian cells (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warburg's original work

claim: Overflow metabolism is ubiquitous among fast-proliferating cells across bacteria, fungi, and mammalian cells.
source: This process, discovered by Otto Warburg in the 1920s (Warburg, 1924) and known as the Warburg effect, aerobic glycolysis, or overflow metabolism (Basan et al., 2015; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009), is ubiquitous among fast-proliferating cells across a broad spectrum of organisms (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), ranging from bacteria (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Meyer et al., 1984; Nanchen et al., 2006; Neidhardt et al., 1990) and fungi (De Deken, 1966) to mammalian cells (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting overflow metabolism across different organisms

claim: Microbes use standard respiration when nutrients are scarce and aerobic glycolysis when nutrients are adequate.
source: For microbes, cells use standard respiration when nutrients are scarce, while they use the counterintuitive aerobic glycolysis when nutrients are adequate, just analogous to normal tissues and cancer cells, respectively (Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on microbial metabolism

claim: Prevalent explanations hold that overflow metabolism arises from proteome efficiency in fermentation being consistently higher than in respiration.
source: Currently, prevalent explanations (Basan et al., 2015; Chen and Nielsen, 2019) hold that overflow metabolism arises from the proteome efficiency in fermentation being consistently higher than that in respiration.
evidence: Supported by citations to existing explanatory frameworks

claim: The measured proteome efficiency in respiration is actually higher than in fermentation for many yeast and cancer cells.
source: However, recent studies have shown that the measured proteome efficiency in respiration is actually higher than in fermentation for many yeast and cancer cells (Shen et al., 2024), even though these cells generate fermentation products through aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent experimental study

claim: The finding that proteome efficiency in respiration is higher than in fermentation contradicts prevalent explanations of overflow metabolism.
source: This finding (Shen et al., 2024) apparently contradicts the prevalent explanations (Basan et al., 2015; Chen and Nielsen, 2019).
evidence: Based on logical inference from comparing recent findings with existing explanations

claim: Most explanations of overflow metabolism rely on the assumption that cells optimize their growth rate for a given rate of carbon influx.
source: Furthermore, most explanations (Basan et al., 2015; Chen and Nielsen, 2019; Majewski and Domach, 1990; Shlomi et al., 2011; Varma and Palsson, 1994; Vazquez et al., 2010; Vazquez and Oltvai, 2016; Zhuang et al., 2011) rely on the assumption that cells optimize their growth rate for a given rate of carbon influx (i.e. nutrient uptake rate) under each nutrient condition (or its equivalents).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple explanatory models

claim: The given factors in a nutrient condition are the identities and concentrations of carbon sources, rather than the carbon influx.
source: However, this assumption remains open to further scrutiny, as the given factors in a nutrient condition are the identities and concentrations of the carbon sources (Molenaar et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019), rather than the carbon influx.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on nutrient conditions and growth optimization

claim: The origin and function of overflow metabolism remain unclear.
source: Therefore, the origin and function of overflow metabolism still remain unclear (DeBerardinis and Chandel, 2020; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to review literature acknowledging the unresolved nature of the problem

claim: There is evolutionary pressure on unicellular organisms to optimize cellular resources for rapid growth.
source: For unicellular organisms, there is evolutionary pressure (Vander Heiden et al., 2009) to optimize cellular resources for rapid growth (Dekel and Alon, 2005; Edwards et al., 2001; Hui et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2010; Towbin et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019; You et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to evolutionary and systems biology literature

claim: Cells allocate protein resources for optimal growth.
source: In particular, it has been shown that cells allocate protein resources for optimal growth (Hui et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019; You et al., 2013), and the most efficient protein allocation corresponds to elementary flux mode (Müller et al., 2014; Wortel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on protein allocation and flux balance analysis

claim: The most efficient protein allocation corresponds to elementary flux mode.
source: In particular, it has been shown that cells allocate protein resources for optimal growth (Hui et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019; You et al., 2013), and the most efficient protein allocation corresponds to elementary flux mode (Müller et al., 2014; Wortel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on elementary flux modes

claim: Disrupting the growth control system and evading immune destruction are prominent hallmarks of cancer cell survival.
source: For cancer cells, disrupting the growth control system and evading immune destruction from the host are prominent hallmarks of their survival (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011), which in certain ways mimic the evolutionary pressure on microbes to optimize cell growth rate.
evidence: Supported by citation to hallmarks of cancer literature

claim: Cancer cells mimic the evolutionary pressure on microbes to optimize cell growth rate.
source: For cancer cells, disrupting the growth control system and evading immune destruction from the host are prominent hallmarks of their survival (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011), which in certain ways mimic the evolutionary pressure on microbes to optimize cell growth rate.
evidence: Based on inference from comparing cancer cell behavior to microbial growth optimization

claim: Overflow metabolism can be understood from optimal protein allocation combined with heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates.
source: In this study, we apply the optimal growth principle of microbes, which also roughly holds for cancer cells, to a heterogeneous framework to address the puzzle of aerobic glycolysis. We use Escherichia coli as a typical example to show that overflow metabolism can be understood from optimal protein allocation combined with heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates.
evidence: This is the main theoretical claim of the study, supported by the model developed in the manuscript

claim: The optimal growth strategy varies between respiration and fermentation depending on the concentration and type of nutrient.
source: The optimal growth strategy varies between respiration and fermentation depending on the concentration and type of the nutrient, and the combination with cell heterogeneity results in the standard picture (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Meyer et al., 1984; Nanchen et al., 2006; van Hoek et al., 1998) of overflow metabolism.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model, with citations to experimental observations

claim: The model quantitatively illustrates the growth rate dependence of fermentation/respiration flux and enzyme allocation under various perturbations in E. coli.
source: Our model quantitatively illustrates the growth rate dependence of fermentation/respiration flux and enzyme allocation under various types of perturbations in E. coli.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model predictions compared with experimental data throughout the Results section

claim: The model provides a quantitative explanation for the Crabtree effect in yeast and the Warburg effect in cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, it provides a quantitative explanation for the data on the Crabtree effect in yeast and the Warburg effect in cancer cells (Bartman et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data from cited studies

claim: Carbon sources that enter from the upper part of glycolysis are classified into Group A.
source: Based on the topology of the metabolic network (Neidhardt et al., 1990; Nelson and Cox, 2008) (see Figure 1A), we classify the carbon sources that enter from the upper part of glycolysis into Group A (Wang et al., 2019) and the precursors of biomass components (such as amino acids) into five pools.
evidence: Based on established metabolic network topology with citation support and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Precursors of biomass components are designated into five pools: a1, a2, b, c, and d based on their entry points.
source: Specifically, each pool is designated according to its entry point (see Figure 1A and Appendix 2.2 for details): a1 (entry point: G6P/F6P), a2 (entry point: GA3P/3PG/PEP), b (entry point: pyruvate/acetyl-CoA), c (entry point: α-ketoglutarate), and d (entry point: oxaloacetate).
evidence: Based on metabolic network structure shown in Figure 1A

claim: The coarse-grained model in Figure 1B is topologically identical to the metabolic network in Figure 1A.
source: Then, the metabolic network for Group A carbon source utilization (see Figure 1A) can be coarse-grained into a model shown in Figure 1B (see Appendix 3.1 for details), where node A represents an arbitrary carbon source of Group A. Evidently, Figure 1B is topologically identical to Figure 1A.
evidence: Direct statement comparing the two figures

claim: The stoichiometric flux Ji scales with the cell population.
source: In fact, the stoichiometric flux Ji scales with the cell population.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the model formulation

claim: Each normalized flux Ji(N) is characterized by the proteomic mass fraction φi and the substrate quality κi, such that Ji(N)=φi⋅κi.
source: In practice, each Ji(N) is characterized by two quantities: the proteomic mass fraction ϕi of the enzyme dedicated to carrying the flux and the substrate quality κi, such that Ji(N)=ϕi⋅κi.
evidence: This is a theoretical formulation in the model

claim: The nutrient quality κA is a variable that depends on the nutrient type and concentration of a Group A carbon source.
source: However, the nutrient quality κA is a variable that depends on the nutrient type and concentration of a Group A carbon source (see Equation S27).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the model formulation

claim: There are three independent fates for a Group A carbon source: fermentation, respiration, and biomass generation.
source: Generally, there are three independent fates for a Group A carbon source in the metabolic network (Chen and Nielsen, 2019): fermentation, respiration, and biomass generation (see Appendix 1—figure 1C-E).
evidence: Based on metabolic network structure with citation support

claim: Each fate (fermentation, respiration, biomass generation) draws a distinct proteome fraction with no overlap between them.
source: Each draws a distinct proteome fraction of ϕf, ϕr and ϕBM, with no overlap between them (see Appendix 3.1).
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption in the model

claim: Ribosomes serve as the factories for protein synthesis and are primarily composed of proteins.
source: During cell proliferation, ribosomes serve as the factories for protein synthesis and are primarily composed of proteins (Neidhardt et al., 1990; Nelson and Cox, 2008), while other biomass components, such as RNA, are optimally produced (Kostinski and Reuveni, 2020) in accordance with the growth rate determined by protein synthesis.
evidence: Based on established cell biology knowledge with citation support

claim: The cell growth rate is proportional to the proteomic mass fraction of active ribosome-affiliated proteins.
source: Thus, the cell growth rate is proportional to ϕR: λ=ϕR⋅κt, where κt is a parameter set by the translation rate (Scott et al., 2010) (see Appendix 2.1 for details), which can be approximated as a constant within the growth rate range of interest (Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on theoretical modeling with citation support

claim: The translation rate parameter κt can be approximated as a constant within the growth rate range of interest.
source: Thus, the cell growth rate is proportional to ϕR: λ=ϕR⋅κt, where κt is a parameter set by the translation rate (Scott et al., 2010) (see Appendix 2.1 for details), which can be approximated as a constant within the growth rate range of interest (Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study

claim: For balanced cell growth in bacteria, the energy demand is generally proportional to the biomass production rate.
source: For balanced cell growth in bacteria, the energy demand JE, expressed as the stoichiometric energy flux in ATP, is generally proportional to the biomass production rate (Ebenhöh et al., 2024), since the proportion of maintenance energy is roughly negligible (Locasale and Cantley, 2010) (see Appendix 10 for the cases of yeast and tumor cells).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on bacterial metabolism

claim: The proportion of maintenance energy is roughly negligible in bacteria.
source: For balanced cell growth in bacteria, the energy demand JE, expressed as the stoichiometric energy flux in ATP, is generally proportional to the biomass production rate (Ebenhöh et al., 2024), since the proportion of maintenance energy is roughly negligible (Locasale and Cantley, 2010) (see Appendix 10 for the cases of yeast and tumor cells).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on maintenance energy

claim: Respiration is significantly more efficient than fermentation in terms of energy biogenesis per unit of carbon.
source: It is well established that respiration is significantly more efficient than fermentation in terms of energy biogenesis per unit of carbon (i.e. βr(A)>βf(A)) (Nelson and Cox, 2008; Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge with citation support

claim: If the proteome efficiency in fermentation is higher than in respiration, the optimal growth strategy is to solely use fermentation.
source: Conversely, if εf>εr, then ϕr=Jr(E)=0 is optimal, and the cell solely uses fermentation.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the optimization model

claim: The choice between respiration and fermentation for growth optimization is determined by comparing their proteome efficiencies.
source: In either case, the choice between respiration and fermentation for growth optimization is determined by comparing their proteome efficiencies.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion from the model analysis

claim: Both proteome efficiencies εr and εf are functions of nutrient quality κA.
source: In practice, both proteome efficiencies εr and εf are functions of nutrient quality κA, which can be significantly influenced by the nutrient type and concentration of the carbon source (see Equations 4 and S27).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the model formulation

claim: In nutrient-poor conditions, the proteome efficiency of respiration is higher than that of fermentation.
source: In nutrient-poor conditions where κA≪κr(A) and κA≪κf(A), the proteome efficiencies can be approximated by εr≈βr(A)⋅κA and εf≈βf(A)⋅κA (see Equation 4), and hence εr(κA)>εf(κA) (since βr(A)>βf(A)), meaning that the proteome efficiency of respiration is higher than that of fermentation under these conditions.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model equations

claim: In rich media, the proteome efficiency in fermentation is higher than that in respiration for E. coli in glucose at saturated concentration.
source: In contrast, in rich media, using parameters for κi derived from in vivo/in vitro experimental data for E. coli (see Appendix 1—table 1, Appendix 1—table 2 and Appendix 7.1–7.2), we obtain εr(κglucose(ST))<εf(κglucose(ST)) with Equation 4 (see also Equations S39-S40), where κglucose(ST) represents the substrate quality of glucose at saturated concentration (abbreviated as 'ST' in the superscript).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on experimental parameter values

claim: The measured proteome efficiency in fermentation is higher than in respiration for E. coli in lactose at saturated concentration.
source: Indeed, recent studies have validated that the measured proteome efficiency in fermentation is higher than in respiration for E. coli in lactose at saturated concentration (Basan et al., 2015), i.e., εr(κlactose(ST))<εf(κlactose(ST)).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study

claim: The ratio Δ(κA)≡εf(κA)/εr(κA) is a monotonically increasing function of κA.
source: Furthermore, the ratio Δ (defined as Δ(κA)≡εf(κA)/εr(κA)) is a monotonically increasing function of κA, and there exists a critical value of κA (denoted as κA(C); see Appendix 3.2 for details) satisfying Δ(κA(C))=1.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model equations

claim: There exists a critical value of nutrient quality κA(C) where the proteome efficiencies of fermentation and respiration are equal.
source: Furthermore, the ratio Δ (defined as Δ(κA)≡εf(κA)/εr(κA)) is a monotonically increasing function of κA, and there exists a critical value of κA (denoted as κA(C); see Appendix 3.2 for details) satisfying Δ(κA(C))=1.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model

claim: Below the critical nutrient quality κA(C), respiration is the optimal choice for cell growth.
source: Below κA(C), where the nutrient is poorer and the cell grows slowly, the proteome efficiency of fermentation is lower than that of respiration (i.e. εf<εr), hence respiration is the optimal choice (with λ=ϕmax⋅(ψ+φ/εr)−1).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the optimization model

claim: Above the critical nutrient quality κA(C), fermentation becomes the optimal growth strategy.
source: Above κA(C), where the nutrient is richer and the cell grows faster, fermentation is more efficient than respiration in terms of proteome efficiency (i.e. εf>εr) and becomes the optimal growth strategy (with λ=ϕmax⋅(ψ+φ/εf)−1).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the optimization model

claim: The analysis qualitatively explains the phenomenon of aerobic glycolysis.
source: This analysis qualitatively explains the phenomenon of aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the theoretical model

claim: In the homogeneous case with optimal protein allocation, the fermentation flux exhibits a digital (step function) response to growth rate.
source: For a quantitative understanding of overflow metabolism, let us first consider the homogeneous case, where all cells share identical biochemical parameters. For optimal protein allocation, the relation between fermentation flux and growth rate under nutrient variation (with significantly varying κA) is given by Jf(E)=φ⋅λ⋅θ(λ−λC), where 'θ' represents the Heaviside step function, and λC denotes the critical growth rate corresponding to the nutrient condition with nutrient quality κA(C) (i.e.  λC≡λ(κA(C))).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the homogeneous model

claim: The digital response outcomes in the homogeneous case are consistent with the numerical simulation findings of Molenaar et al., 2009.
source: These digital response outcomes are consistent with the numerical simulation findings of Molenaar et al., 2009.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous modeling study

claim: The digital response in the homogeneous case is incompatible with the threshold-analog response observed in overflow metabolism.
source: However, they are clearly incompatible with the threshold-analog response observed in the standard picture of overflow metabolism (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Meyer et al., 1984; Nanchen et al., 2006; van Hoek et al., 1998).
evidence: Based on comparison with experimental observations cited

claim: Cell heterogeneity is ubiquitous in both microbes and tumor cells.
source: To address this issue, we take into account cell heterogeneity, which is ubiquitous in both microbes (Ackermann, 2015; Bagamery et al., 2020; Balaban et al., 2004; Nikolic et al., 2013; Solopova et al., 2014; Wallden et al., 2016; Yaginuma et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018) and tumor cells (Duraj et al., 2021; Shibao et al., 2018; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Hensley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Experimental studies have reported significant metabolic heterogeneity in the choice between respiration and fermentation within a cell population.
source: In the context of the Warburg effect or overflow metabolism, experimental studies have reported significant metabolic heterogeneity in the choice between respiration and fermentation within a cell population (Bagamery et al., 2020; Duraj et al., 2021; Shibao et al., 2018; Hensley et al., 2016; Nikolic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: The turnover number (kcat value) of a catalytic enzyme varies considerably between in vitro and in vivo measurements.
source: Motivated by the observation that the turnover number (kcat value) of a catalytic enzyme varies considerably between in vitro and in vivo measurements (Davidi et al., 2016; García-Contreras et al., 2012), we note that the concentrations of potassium and phosphate, which vary from cell to cell, have a significant impact on the kcat values of metabolic enzymes (García-Contreras et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: The concentrations of potassium and phosphate have a significant impact on the kcat values of metabolic enzymes.
source: Motivated by the observation that the turnover number (kcat value) of a catalytic enzyme varies considerably between in vitro and in vivo measurements (Davidi et al., 2016; García-Contreras et al., 2012), we note that the concentrations of potassium and phosphate, which vary from cell to cell, have a significant impact on the kcat values of metabolic enzymes (García-Contreras et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study

claim: Within a cell population, there is a distribution of kcat values for a catalytic enzyme, referred to as extrinsic noise.
source: Therefore, within a cell population, there is a distribution of kcat values for a catalytic enzyme, commonly referred to as extrinsic noise (Elowitz et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on inference from enzyme variability with citation to noise literature

claim: The kcat values for each enzyme follow a Gaussian distribution in the model.
source: For simplicity, we assume that the kcat values for each enzyme follow a Gaussian distribution.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption

claim: The proteome efficiencies εr and εf follow Gaussian distributions due to enzyme heterogeneity.
source: Consequently, the proteome efficiencies εr and εf, which are crucial for determining the choice between respiration and fermentation, also follow Gaussian distributions (see Appendix 8 for details).
evidence: This is a theoretical consequence of the Gaussian assumption for enzyme kcat values

claim: The variability in proteome efficiencies leads to diverse distributions of single-cell growth rates across different carbon sources.
source: This variability leads to diverse distributions of single-cell growth rates across different carbon sources (see Equations S155-S157 and S163-S165), which has been fully verified by recent experiments using isogenic E. coli at single-cell resolution (Wallden et al., 2016; see Appendix 1—figure 2B).
evidence: Theoretical prediction verified by experimental data

claim: Assuming the coefficient of variation of λC is 12% is equivalent to assuming the CV for the catalytic rate of each metabolic enzyme is 25%.
source: Assuming the coefficient of variation (CV) of λC is σλC/μC=12%, or equivalently that the CV for the catalytic rate of each metabolic enzyme is 25%, we derive the growth rate dependence of fermentation and respiration fluxes (see Appendix 3.3 for details):
evidence: This is a modeling assumption used to fit the data

claim: The fermentation flux exhibits a threshold-analog relation with the growth rate when cell heterogeneity is incorporated.
source: The fermentation flux exhibits a threshold-analog relation with the growth rate (the red curves in Figures 1C–D—3B, D and F), while the respiration flux (the blue curve in Figure 1D) decreases as the fermentation flux increases.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction shown in the figures

claim: The model results quantitatively agree with experimental data from E. coli for fermentation and respiration fluxes.
source: In Figure 1C–D, we observe that the model results (see Equation 5 and Appendix 9 for details; parameters are set based on the experimental data shown in Appendix 1—table 1) quantitatively agree with the experimental data from E. coli (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in figures

claim: By incorporating cell heterogeneity, the model of optimal protein allocation quantitatively explains overflow metabolism.
source: By incorporating cell heterogeneity, our model of optimal protein allocation quantitatively explains overflow metabolism.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's explanatory power

claim: The net effect of φZ perturbation is that the maximum fraction of the proteome available for resource allocation changes from φmax to φmax−φZ.
source: The net effect of the ϕZ perturbation is that the maximum fraction of the proteome available for resource allocation changes from ϕmax to ϕmax−ϕZ (Basan et al., 2015), where ϕZ is the proteomic mass fraction of useless proteins.
evidence: Based on the nature of the perturbation with citation support

claim: For each degree of LacZ expression, the fermentation flux exhibits a threshold-analog response to growth rate as κA varies.
source: For each degree of LacZ expression (with fixed ϕZ), similar to wild-type strains, the fermentation flux exhibits a threshold-analog response to growth rate as κA varies (see Figure 2C), which agrees quantitatively with experimental results (Basan et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data

claim: The scaling relations for φZ perturbation are well validated by experimental data.
source: These scaling relations are well validated by the experimental data (Basan et al., 2015) shown in Figure 2B.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in figure

claim: In the case where both κA and φZ vary, experimental data points lie on the predicted threshold-analog response surface.
source: Finally, in the case where both κA and ϕZ are free to vary, the growth rate dependence of fermentation flux presents a threshold-analog response surface in a 3D plot, where ϕZ appears explicitly as the y-axis (see Figure 2A). Experimental data points (Basan et al., 2015) lie right on this surface, which is highly consistent with the model predictions.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in 3D plot

claim: Energy dissipation introduces an energy dissipation coefficient w to the energy demand equation.
source: Next, we study the influence of energy dissipation, which introduces an energy dissipation coefficient w to Equation 2: JE(N)=ηE⋅λ+w.
evidence: This is a model modification to account for energy dissipation

claim: The model results for energy dissipation demonstrate good agreement with experimental data.
source: In Figure 3A–B, we present a comparison between the model results and experimental data (Basan et al., 2015) in 3D and 2D plots, which demonstrate good agreement.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in figures

claim: A notable characteristic of energy dissipation is that the fermentation flux increases despite a decrease in growth rate when κA is fixed.
source: A notable characteristic of energy dissipation, as distinguished from ϕZ perturbation, is that the fermentation flux increases despite a decrease in the growth rate when κA is fixed.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction distinguishing energy dissipation from other perturbations

claim: The model predictions for translation inhibition are generally consistent with experimental data.
source: In Appendix 1—figure 2D and E, we observe that the model predictions are generally consistent with the experimental data (Basan et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data

claim: A noticeable systematic discrepancy arises in the translation inhibition model when the translation rate is low.
source: However, a noticeable systematic discrepancy arises when the translation rate is low.
evidence: Observation from comparing model with data

claim: Maintenance energy is typically tiny and generally negligible for bacteria over the growth rate range of interest.
source: Therefore, we consider maintenance energy, which is typically tiny and generally negligible for bacteria over the growth rate range of interest (Basan et al., 2015; Locasale and Cantley, 2010; Neidhardt, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on bacterial metabolism

claim: Pyruvate enters the metabolic network from the endpoint of glycolysis.
source: Finally, we consider the alteration of nutrient categories by switching to a non-Group A carbon source: pyruvate, which enters the metabolic network from the endpoint of glycolysis (Neidhardt et al., 1990; Nelson and Cox, 2008).
evidence: Based on established metabolic network knowledge with citation support

claim: The coarse-grained model for pyruvate utilization shares identical precursor pools with those for Group A carbon sources.
source: The coarse-grained model for pyruvate utilization is shown in Figure 3E (see also Figure 1A), which shares identical precursor pools with those for Group A carbon sources, yet has several differences in the coarse-grained reactions.
evidence: Based on comparison of model structures shown in figures

claim: The critical growth rate λC(py) for pyruvate utilization is noticeably smaller than that for Group A sources.
source: Most notably, the critical growth rate λC(py) and the ATP production per glucose in the fermentation pathway βf(py) for pyruvate utilization are noticeably smaller than those for Group A sources (i.e. λC and βf(A), respectively).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from comparing model parameters

claim: The growth rate dependence of fermentation flux in pyruvate presents a distinctly different curve from that of Group A carbon sources.
source: Consequently, the growth rate dependence of fermentation flux in pyruvate should present a distinctly different curve from that of Group A carbon sources (see Equations 5 and S105), which is fully validated by experimental results (Holms, 1996; see Figure 3F).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in figure

claim: The coarse-grained model can predict enzyme allocation for each gene in glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
source: As mentioned above, our coarse-grained model is topologically identical to the central metabolic network (see Figure 1A) and can thus predict enzyme allocation for each gene in glycolysis and the TCA cycle (see Appendix 1—figure 1B and Appendix 1—table 1) under various types of perturbations.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's predictive capability

claim: φ1 and φ2 correspond to enzymes involved in glycolysis or at the junction of glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
source: Therefore, ϕ1 and ϕ2 correspond to enzymes involved in glycolysis (or at the junction of glycolysis and the TCA cycle), while ϕ3 and ϕ4 correspond to enzymes in the TCA cycle (see Figure 1A–B and Appendix 3.1).
evidence: Based on the mapping between coarse-grained model and metabolic network

claim: φ3 and φ4 correspond to enzymes in the TCA cycle.
source: Therefore, ϕ1 and ϕ2 correspond to enzymes involved in glycolysis (or at the junction of glycolysis and the TCA cycle), while ϕ3 and ϕ4 correspond to enzymes in the TCA cycle (see Figure 1A–B and Appendix 3.1).
evidence: Based on the mapping between coarse-grained model and metabolic network

claim: The growth rate dependence of enzyme allocation under κA perturbation is generally described by a C-line response in simplified models.
source: This has been extensively studied in more simplified models (Hui et al., 2015; You et al., 2013), where the growth rate dependence of enzyme allocation under κA perturbation is generally described by a C-line response (Hui et al., 2015; You et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous modeling studies

claim: Genes responsible for digesting carbon compounds exhibit a linear increase in gene expression as the growth rate decreases.
source: Specifically, the genes responsible for digesting carbon compounds exhibit a linear increase in gene expression as the growth rate decreases (Hui et al., 2015; You et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Enzymes in glycolysis exhibit a completely different response pattern compared to those in the TCA cycle under κA perturbation.
source: However, when it comes to enzymes catalyzing reactions between intermediate nodes, we gathered experimental data from existing studies (Hui et al., 2015) and found that the enzymes in glycolysis exhibit a completely different response pattern compared to those in the TCA cycle (see Appendix 1—figure 3A and B).
evidence: Based on analysis of experimental data from cited study

claim: The C-line response cannot explain the discrepancy between glycolysis and TCA cycle enzyme responses.
source: This discrepancy cannot be explained by the C-line response.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental observations with existing model predictions

claim: The model predictions overall match with experimental data for representative genes from either glycolysis or the TCA cycle under κA perturbation.
source: In Figure 4A–B and Appendix 1—figure 3C-D, we see that the model predictions overall match with the experimental data (Hui et al., 2015) for representative genes from either glycolysis or the TCA cycle, and maintenance energy (with w0=2.5(h−1)) has a negligible effect on this process.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in figures

claim: Minor discrepancies in enzyme allocation predictions arise from the basal expression of metabolic genes.
source: Still, there are minor discrepancies that arise from the basal expression of metabolic genes, which may be attributed to the fact that our model deals with relatively stable growth conditions while microbes need to be prepared for fluctuating environments (Basan et al., 2020; Kussell and Leibler, 2005; Mori et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on inference about model limitations with citation support

claim: For φZ perturbation, the model predicts a linear response to growth rate reduction for all genes in either glycolysis or the TCA cycle.
source: We proceed to analyze the influence of ϕZ perturbation and energy dissipation. In both cases, our model predicts a linear response to growth rate reduction for all genes in either glycolysis or the TCA cycle (see Appendix 6.2–6.3 for details).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model

claim: For φZ perturbation, all predicted slopes are positive.
source: For ϕZ perturbation, all predicted slopes are positive, and there are no fitting parameters involved (Equations S120-S121).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model

claim: The model quantitatively illustrates experimental data for representative genes in the central metabolic network under φZ perturbation.
source: In Figure 4C–D and Appendix 1—figure 3E-J, we show that our model quantitatively illustrates the experimental data (Basan et al., 2015) for representative genes in the central metabolic network, and there is a better agreement with experiments (Basan et al., 2015) by incorporating the maintenance energy (with w0=2.5(h−1) as aforementioned).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in figures

claim: For energy dissipation, the predicted slopes of enzymes corresponding to φ4 are negative.
source: For energy dissipation, however, the predicted slopes of the enzymes corresponding to ϕ4 are negative, and there is a constraint that the slope signs of the enzymes corresponding to the same ϕi (i=1,2,3) should be the same.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model

claim: The model results for energy dissipation are consistent with experiments.
source: In Appendix 1—figure 3K-N, we see that the model results (Equations S127 and S123) are consistent with experiments (Basan et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data

claim: For yeast and tumors, the proteome efficiencies εr and εf are both increasing functions of nutrient quality κA.
source: For yeast and tumors, similar to the case of E. coli, the proteome efficiencies εr and εf are both increasing functions of nutrient quality κA (see Equation S170).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from applying the model to yeast and tumors

claim: Under poor nutrient conditions, the proteome efficiency in respiration is higher than in fermentation for yeast and tumors.
source: Under poor nutrient conditions (i.e. κA is small), the proteome efficiency in respiration is higher than that in fermentation: εr>εf (see Equations S174-S175), making respiration the optimal choice for growth optimization (see Equation S171).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model applied to yeast and tumors

claim: When nutrients are abundant for yeast and tumors, aerobic glycolysis becomes the optimal growth strategy.
source: Conversely, when nutrients are abundant and εf>εr, aerobic glycolysis (i.e. fermentation) becomes the optimal growth strategy (see Equation S172).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model applied to yeast and tumors

claim: The standard picture of overflow metabolism has been observed in yeast.
source: Further combination with cell heterogeneity results in the standard picture of overflow metabolism, which has indeed been observed in yeast (van Hoek et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study on yeast

claim: It remains challenging to tune the growth rate of cancer cells in vivo.
source: However, it remains challenging to tune the growth rate of cancer cells in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental limitations

claim: Shen et al., 2024 discovered that the proteome efficiency in respiration is higher than in fermentation for many yeast and cancer cells at the population level.
source: Recently, Shen et al., 2024 discovered that the proteome efficiency measured at the cell population level in respiration (i.e. ⟨εr⟩ ; where '⟨⟩' denotes the population average) is higher than that in fermentation (i.e. ⟨εf⟩) for many yeast and cancer cells, despite the presence of fermentation fluxes through aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent experimental study

claim: The finding by Shen et al., 2024 contradicts prevalent explanations of overflow metabolism.
source: Evidently, this finding (Shen et al., 2024) contradicts prevalent explanations (Basan et al., 2015; Chen and Nielsen, 2019), which hold that overflow metabolism arises because the proteome efficiency in fermentation is consistently higher than in respiration.
evidence: Based on logical comparison of findings with existing explanations

claim: The model may resolve the puzzle raised by Shen et al., 2024 due to incorporation of two important features.
source: Nevertheless, our model may resolve this puzzle due to the incorporation of two important features.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's explanatory power

claim: The model predicts that proteome efficiency in respiration is larger than in fermentation when nutrient quality is low.
source: First, our model predicts that the proteome efficiency in respiration is larger than that in fermentation when nutrient quality is low (see Equations S174-S175).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model

claim: By accounting for cell heterogeneity, the model allows a proportion of cells to have higher proteome efficiency in fermentation than respiration even when the overall population-level efficiency in respiration is greater.
source: Second, and crucially, by accounting for cell heterogeneity, our model allows a proportion of cells to have a higher proteome efficiency in fermentation than in respiration, even when the overall proteome efficiency in respiration at the cell population level is greater than that in fermentation (i.e. ⟨εr⟩>⟨εf⟩).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the heterogeneity model

claim: The theoretical results with χεr=χεf=0.58 align quantitatively with experimental data on yeast and mouse tumors.
source: As shown in Figure 5A–B, the theoretical results with χεr=χεf=0.58 align quantitatively with the experimental data (Bartman et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024) on both logarithmic and linear scales, demonstrating that our model has the potential to quantitatively explain the Crabtree effect in yeast and the Warburg effect in cancer cells.
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in figures

claim: Under nutrient-poor conditions, the proteome efficiency of respiration is higher than that of fermentation, and thus the cell uses respiration to optimize growth.
source: Under nutrient-poor conditions, the proteome efficiency of respiration is higher than that of fermentation (see Figure 1E), and thus the cell uses respiration to optimize growth.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's main finding with reference to figure

claim: In rich media, the proteome efficiency of fermentation increases more rapidly and surpasses that of respiration, leading the cell to adopt fermentation as the optimal growth strategy.
source: In rich media, however, the proteome efficiency of fermentation increases more rapidly and surpasses that of respiration (see Figure 1E), leading the cell to adopt fermentation as the optimal growth strategy.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's main finding with reference to figure

claim: The model quantitatively illustrates the threshold-analog response in overflow metabolism when combined with cell heterogeneity.
source: In further combination with cell heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates (Davidi et al., 2016; García-Contreras et al., 2012), our model quantitatively illustrates the threshold-analog response (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996) in overflow metabolism (see Figure 1C).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data with citation support

claim: The cAMP-CRP system plays a crucial role in sensing proteome efficiency and executing the optimal strategy.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that the cyclic AMP (cAMP)-cAMP receptor protein (CRP) system plays a crucial role in sensing proteome efficiency and executing the optimal strategy (Basan et al., 2015; Towbin et al., 2017; Valgepea et al., 2010; Wehrens et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: The cAMP-CRP system alone is insufficient, and additional regulators remain to be identified.
source: However, it has also been suggested that the cAMP-CRP system alone is insufficient, and that additional regulators remain to be identified to fully elucidate this mechanism (Basan et al., 2015; Valgepea et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on regulatory mechanisms

claim: The optimal growth principle in the model can be relaxed to cases where efficient protein allocation is required only for enzymes, rather than ribosomes.
source: Furthermore, since the binary choice between respiration and fermentation is driven by the comparison of proteome efficiencies, the optimal growth principle in our model can be relaxed to the case where efficient protein allocation is required only for enzymes, rather than ribosomes.
evidence: This is a theoretical extension of the model

claim: The model remains applicable under suboptimal growth conditions where the inactive portion of ribosomes may vary.
source: This allows our model to remain applicable under suboptimal growth conditions (see Appendix 3.4 for details), where recent experimental studies have shown that the inactive portion of ribosomes (i.e. ribosomes not bound to mRNAs) may vary with culturing conditions (Dai et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018) and between individual cells within the same culture (Pavlou et al., 2025), despite an overall trend toward growth optimization.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on ribosome activity

claim: In existing rationales, the standard picture of overflow metabolism has primarily been illustrated by a threshold-linear response.
source: In existing rationales (Basan et al., 2015; Chen and Nielsen, 2019; Majewski and Domach, 1990; Shlomi et al., 2011; Varma and Palsson, 1994; Vazquez et al., 2010; Vazquez and Oltvai, 2016), the standard picture of overflow metabolism (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Meyer et al., 1984; Nanchen et al., 2006; van Hoek et al., 1998) has primarily been illustrated by a threshold-linear response, which largely relies on the assumption that cells optimize their growth rate for a given rate of carbon influx under each nutrient condition (or similar equivalents; see Appendix 7.3).
evidence: Supported by citations to existing modeling approaches

claim: For microbes or tumor cells grown in vitro or in vivo, the given factors are the identity and concentration of the nutrient, rather than the rate of carbon influx.
source: However, in practice, for microbes or tumor cells grown in vitro or in vivo, the given factors are the identity and concentration of the nutrient (Molenaar et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019), rather than the rate of carbon influx.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on growth conditions

claim: The model differs from existing rationales by optimizing cell growth rate purely through protein allocation without imposing a special constraint on carbon influx.
source: Our model resolves this puzzle by significantly differing from existing rationales in its optimization principle, where we optimize cell growth rate purely through protein allocation without imposing a special constraint on carbon influx (see Appendix 7.3 for details).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's theoretical approach

claim: Cell heterogeneity is crucial for both explaining the threshold-analog response in overflow metabolism and for resolving the puzzle raised by Shen et al., 2024.
source: More importantly, our model incorporates cell heterogeneity, which is crucial for both explaining the threshold-analog response in overflow metabolism and for resolving this puzzle raised by Shen et al., 2024.
evidence: This is a claim about the importance of heterogeneity in the model

claim: In the homogeneous case, cells would not generate fermentation flux if the proteome efficiency in fermentation were lower than in respiration under the optimal growth framework.
source: Furthermore, in this case, cells would not generate fermentation flux if the proteome efficiency in fermentation were lower than that in respiration, under the optimal growth framework.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the homogeneous model

claim: By incorporating heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates, the critical growth rate shifts from a single value to a Gaussian distribution across a cell population.
source: By incorporating heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates (Davidi et al., 2016; García-Contreras et al., 2012), the critical growth rate (i.e. threshold) shifts from a single value to a Gaussian distribution (see Equation S45 and Appendix 8 for details; see also Appendix 1—figure 4) across a cell population, thereby turning a digital response into the threshold-analog response observed in overflow metabolism (see Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction with citation support

claim: The model results are supported by observed distributions of single-cell growth rates in E. coli.
source: Our model results, based on cell heterogeneity, are further supported by observed distributions of single-cell growth rates in E. coli (Wallden et al., 2016) (see Appendix 1—figure 2B), as well as by experiments involving various types of perturbations (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Hui et al., 2015), both in terms of acetate secretion patterns and gene expression in the central metabolic network (see Figures 2—4, Appendix 1—figures 2D and E and 3).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: The heterogeneity patterns predicted by the model are highly consistent with non-genetic heterogeneity observed in single-cell experiments with E. coli and S. cerevisiae.
source: Furthermore, the heterogeneity patterns predicted by our model for fermentation and respiration modes in an isogenic cell population under the same culturing conditions are highly consistent with the non-genetic heterogeneity observed in single-cell experiments with E. coli (Nikolic et al., 2013) and S. cerevisiae (Bagamery et al., 2020), and align with experiments on intra-tumor heterogeneity in glioblastoma (Duraj et al., 2021; Shibao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on heterogeneity

claim: The model can be broadly applied to address heterogeneity-related challenges in metabolism on a quantitative basis.
source: Finally, our model can be broadly applied to address heterogeneity-related challenges in metabolism on a quantitative basis, including diverse metabolic strategies of cells in various environments (Bagamery et al., 2020; Duraj et al., 2021; Escalante-Chong et al., 2015; Hensley et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2015; Solopova et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's broader applicability with citation support
